newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Clinton win augurs Sino-U.S. thaw, small HK impact.
newsitem.headline: Clinton win augurs Sino-U.S. thaw, small HK impact.

text.p: Bill Clinton's re-election will have little impact on Hong Kong as the British colony heads for Chinese rule next year, but dialogue between Washington and China is likely to gather pace, analysts said on Wednesday.
Beijing's mouthpiece newspapers in Hong Kong said they expected positive changes in U.S. policy towards China.

The daily Wen Wei Po said U.S. policy would be adjusted because Washington had realised that isolating China would harm its own strategic interests. It said the U.S. had realised Asia would be the most prosperous region in the world, led by China.
"It's not going to affect us a great deal," Hong Kong-based China analyst Tai-Ming Cheung told Reuters.

"The main thing now is who is going to take over the foreign policy and security portfolios," Cheung said. The secretary of state, secretary of defence and the national security adviser were all expected to be replaced in Clinton's second term.
"It's a question of whether you have people who are familiar with China issues coming on board," he said. "China remains fairly low down in the next administration's priorities."

Cheung said the U.S. had taken a clearly more positive approach to China recently. "The whole emphasis now is on the strategic dialogue between China and the U.S. So you're going to get a lot more high-level meetings taking place.
"The big issue is when the U.S. President will go to visit China. It doesn't seem that's going to happen until after the handover of Hong Kong," Cheung said.
The British colony reverts to Chinese sovereignty as a special region next July 1, and Washington has said it hopes to see the territory's basic freedoms survive the change of flag.
"The focus now is to have this dialogue so that both sides can talk more knowledgeably to each other, Cheung said."
Some China analysts said the Sino-U.S. relationship would continue to be influenced by the composition of Congress.
If the Republicans continued to dominate Congress, China's human rights record would remain in sharp focus, they said.
The Republicans might try to relink China's tenure of most favoured nation (MFN) trade status to human rights concessions.
Mark Michaelson, chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said Clinton's victory over Bob Dole would make little difference to Sino-U.S. ties.
